Not all code needs to be converted to functions
Under the correct conditions, a replicate()is a good substitute for a for()since replicate is vectorized and for() is not.
The output of the last command in the body is the output of the function.
If the last command does not have an output nothing will be returned
R does have a return() statement that is optional. An R function with a return() will output whatever you specify and then immediately exit/end the function.
A function can only return one object. To return multiple objects, store them in a list first.

section: Plotting in Base R with plot()
text:
Plotting in Base R with plot()
The function plot() is the place to start because many other basic graphing functions use its arguments. plot() is a generic function, which means that it can be used to create many different types of plots depending on the type of data you give it. For example, rivers is a simple vector of the lengths of 141 rivers in the United States. If you give it to plot() it will create a scatterplot of the lengths of the rivers. The x-axis will be the index of the river (1, 2, 3, etc.) and the y-axis will be the length of the river.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Compare it to cars which is a simple data frame consisting of two columns:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You could insert an entire data frame into plot() and it will create a scatterplot matrix (this can also be accomplished with the function pairs()):

Extracting Specific Data Vectors
Typically, we have many more columns than our last two examples. In that case, we need to extract the specific columns we want to plot. For example, suppose we wish to plot the relationship between Sepal.Length and Petal.Length in the iris data set. We can extract these columns using the $ operator and then plot them against each other. All three of the next plots are the same, only the manner of calling each vector is different.

title: Week 4 Data Viz Part 1
text:
The Graphical Parameters

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
There are over 100, but you would only change a few. Most likely (no particular order):


col (color of points, lines, etc.)

pch (point character, the shape of the points)

cex (character expansion, the size of points, lines, etc.)

lwd (line width, the thickness of lines)

lty (line type, the style of lines)

main (main title of the plot)

xlab (x-axis label)

ylab (y-axis label)

xlim (x-axis limits)

ylim (y-axis limits)

The [1] that you see printed is just an index that R uses to indicate the position of the first element in the output. Since we are just doing simple calculations and there is only one element in the output, it is indexed as [1]. If you were to do a calculation that resulted in multiple values, you would see multiple indices.
R also uses new lines to separate the outputs of different calculations (or complete each expression generally). When you run the code chunk above, you will also see the results of each calculation on a new line.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Built-in datasets in R
No one is going to hire you to program calculations like the ones above, but they will hire you to work with data. R has a lot of built-in data that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Let’s examine iris which is a built-in data set. You can run the code chunk below to see what it looks like.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Let’s unpack this! You can modify my code above in the browser, try modifying the box above with head(iris) instead of just iris and see what happens. head() is a function.
Functions
Functions do all of the work in R. Functions have a function name followed by parentheses. Functions can have arguments and options within the parentheses. So head(iris) reveals the first few rows of the built-in data iris. This is a way to get a quick look at the data without overwhelming you (or anyone else) with all 150 rows.
Examine iris
Notice the row numbering on the left and the column names at the top. The row numbering is just for reference and is not part of the data. By convention, rows typically (not always) represent an observation. The column names are important because they tell you what each column represents. In this case, we have measurements of different parts of the iris flower (sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width) and the species of the flower.
A handy function when you are starting out in R is is() (seriously). It tells you what is this iris thing?
An object is something that R recognizes and knows how to store it in memory and work with when you request the R object by its name. iris is a built-in R object that contains data. We can ask R what type of R object iris is:

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
The vector
In the example of x, y and z, a numeric vector is a sequence of values that are all of the same type (in this case, numbers). In R, the vector (there are different types, later…) is the fundamental data structure.
Notice that for a single number, R still treats it as a vector of length 1 (there are no scalars in R) with index [1]. This is a common source of confusion for those new to R. R is 1-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 1. It is like the way we count. Python, C / C++, Java, JavaScript and many other programming languages are 0-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 0.
You can examine the built-in data set rivers to see an example of a numeric vector. Try it out below and notice the values of the indices between the [].

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
How many values are in the rivers data set? You can check your answer by using the length() function or (for understanding only) by looking at the indices of the last value in rivers.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Back to iris
Remember iris above? It is a data frame, which is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, characters, etc.). Another handy basic function in R is str() which gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object. Try it on iris.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now we are getting a real look at data in R. We see that iris has 150 rows and 5 columns. The first four columns are numeric (the measurements of the flowers) and the last column is a factor (the species of the flower). We will learn more about factors later, but for now, just know that it is a way to store non-numeric (categorical) data (like species).
I am going to leave you with two more useful basic functions, summary(), which gives you a quick summary of an R object. Try it on iris and just for fun, try it on rivers too. What happens and why?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
and finally help() which gives you the documentation for a function or a built in data set like rivers or iris. Try it on head() to see what head() can do and what additional arguments it can take.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Takeaways

R is a fancy calculator that can do basic arithmetic and more complex calculations. Issue a help("Syntax") to see the syntax for basic calculations in R.
R uses line breaks to separate the outputs of different calculations (or complete each expression generally).

You can give a value a name (called a variable, like math), and then use that name (variable) in calculations and to store results.
R has many built-in data sets such as iris and rivers that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Functions do all of the work in R. They have arguments that you can modify to get different results. For example, head() is a function that takes an R (typically) data object as an argument (it can take other kinds of R objects).
The is() function tells you what type of R object you are working with.
The vector is the most basic type of data object in R, and it is a sequence of values that are all of the same type.
The data frame is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, factors, etc.).
R vectors are 1-indexed (numbered starting with 1), even when the vector only has one value (there are no scalars in R, only vectors).
The str() function gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object.
The summary() function gives you a quick summary of the data in each vector (column) of a data frame.

title: Lecture 06
text:
List
From the original documentation

Lists are another kind of data storage. Lists have elements, each of which can contain any type of R object, i.e. the elements of a list do not have to be of the same type. List elements are accessed through three different indexing operations. These are explained in detail in Indexing.

Lists are called “generic vectors”, and the basic vector types (e.g., integer, numeric, character etc.) that we have been using are referred to as “atomic vectors”.

title: Lecture 06
text:
Recall

The data type in our simple vector must be all the same (all numeric, all character, all logical)
If there is mixing, we say that R “coerces” the vector to be one type.
But if data are stored in a list, they can maintain their own type.

title: Lecture 06
section: Why do they do this? Why lists?
text:
Why do they do this? Why lists?

If a programmer wants a single long and complex structure and also wants each piece of it to keep its original type, they use a list to contain all of the pieces.
Recall vectors (atomic ones) coerce the data to keep the type with the highest priority (e.g., logical coerces to integer, integer to numeric, numeric to character etc.)
Many important model objects are lists, like the results of a regression and more advanced models.
Many heavily used functions produce lists

title: Lecture 06
text:
Suggestions

Practice constructing sequences using the colon operator (:) and seq(). Those work on numeric data and can increment and decrement.
Practice constructing any type (logical, character, numeric) using concatenate/combine with c() or even rep()
Practice on simple vectors such as rivers or extract a vector from iris (e.g., iris$Sepal.Width) and then extract specific values
Practice extracting from entire lists, for example, take a subset of rows or of column or both. Then parts of rows, parts of columns.
Work your way up to the list.
Extraction is a bit like solving a puzzle.

title: Lecture 06
text:
Solution (Week 3)

Remove non-numeric characters first, then convert to numeric.
We could remove the characters (like the comma and percentage) in this manner
gsub is a “global substitution” function, it searches for the character we specify and then removes all occurrences.
might be easiest understood reading from the innermost part of the R function


# for commas |> is a "pipe
# The pipe |> means:
# “Take the result on the left and pass it into the function on the right.”"

BOM0024$Worldwide <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Worldwide) |> as.numeric()
BOM0024$Domestic  <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Domestic) |> as.numeric()
BOM0024$Foreign   <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Foreign) |> as.numeric()

# for percent we nested it instead to show the readability of |>
BOM0024$Domestic_percent <- (gsub("%", "", BOM0024$Domestic_percent) |> as.numeric())/100

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

BOM0024$Foreign_percent  <- (gsub("%", "", BOM0024$Foreign_percent) |> as.numeric())/100

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

text:
Joining/Merging

This a fundamental data handling skill which borders on intermediate
As in the previous example, data are broken up into separate files. BUT the information in the columns is different each file and the rows are the same (or mostly the same)
This is a situation where one is trying to augment data on existing observations with additional data on the column dimension (added characteristics, added variables).
Generally, you should want a “key” or an identifier variable/column that you can match your datasets on before doing this.
We are going to get some data for this one

Example Problem #1
replicate() vs for()

SetupReplicateFor Looptabledviz



How would you write a coin toss function where we flip a fair coin 10 times and count the number of heads?
And then repeat this “experiment” 100 times (run the function 100 times)
Could you program it using replicate() ?
How would it differ using a for() loop?
The Pseudocode for the function would look something like

FUNCTION coin_toss()

        create a coin to toss
        toss the coin 10 times
        record the number of heads
        count up the number of heads
        store result

  face <- sample(coin, size = 10, replace = TRUE) # simulate 10 independent tosses

How would you rewrite the coin toss simulator where you allow the function user to modify how many coins and how many trials?
Could you program it using replicate()
How would it differ using a for() loop?
The Pseudocode would look something like

FUNCTION coin_toss2(n, trials)

    REPEAT trials:

        create a coin to toss
        toss the coin n times (user-specified)
        record the number of heads
        count up the number of heads
        store result

    RETURN the results

END FUNCTION




Code
coin_simulator_rep <- function(n, trials) {
  replicate(
    trials,
    sum(sample(c(0, 1), size = n, replace = TRUE))
  )
}

Code
coin_simulator_loop <- function(n, trials) {
  
  results <- numeric(trials)
  
  for (i in seq_len(trials)) {
    tosses <- sample(c(0, 1), size = n, replace = TRUE)
    results[i] <- sum(tosses)
  }
  
  return(results)
}

title: Lecture 12
text:
Example 3: State Dependency

Introinitialize variablesloop



When playing a board game like Monopoly. You roll the die to see how many spaces you move. To know what space you land on for turn 3, you must know exactly what space you were sitting on at the end of turn 2.
The past value matters so replicate() is entirely useless here. The computer must resolve the timeline sequentially using a for().





Code
# Establish rules
number_of_turns <- 10

# Pre-allocate a vector to track board position
# (Braun & Murdoch style)
board_position <- numeric(number_of_turns)

# Set our starting state (Turn 1: start at space 0)
board_position[1] <- 0

# For teaching, keep track of the rolls
roll_value <- numeric(number_of_turns)
roll_value[1] <- 0






Code
# Start looping at turn 2, because turn 1 is already decided.
for (i in 2:number_of_turns) {
  
  # Step 1: An isolated random event (rolling the die)
  roll <- sample(1:6, size = 1)
  roll_value[i] <- roll

  # Step 2: The State Dependency
  # Current Position = Past Position + The Roll
  board_position[i] <- board_position[i - 1] + roll
}

print(roll_value)


 [1] 0 6 3 5 1 1 5 5 5 1


Code
print(board_position)


 [1]  0  6  9 14 15 16 21 26 31 32

} 

system.time({

})

  0.546   0.002   0.548 


Code
system.time({
  results_for <- numeric(trials)
  
  for (i in seq_len(trials)) { # seq_len for numbers
    results_for[i] <- coin_toss()
  }
})

The ‘user time’ is the computer processing time spent on your code. The ‘system time’ is the computer processing time spent by Mac or Windows on your computer to help R with what it needed. Elapsed is what you experience.

title: Lecture 12
text:
for() loop or vectorize code?

Vectorize when the logic is independent and contained within R
Loop when the logic is sequential (dependent), reaches outside of R

1. State Dependency (Recursive Operations)
Vectorized operations assume that each calculation is independent of the others. A for loop is required when iteration \(i\) depends on the result of iteration \(i-1\).

Stochastic Simulations: If you are building a random walk, a Markov chain, or a population model where a future state is calculated using the present state, can’t vectorize (dependent)
Complex Accumulation: If the rules for accumulation change based on the running total (e.g., an account balance that incurs a penalty when it drops below a certain level), a for loop provides the necessary control flow.

title: Lecture 12
text:
for() loop or vectorize code?
2. Working with “The Outside World”
Vectorization is designed to work with data inside R’s memory. When your want to interact with the environment outside of R the for loop is the correct tool.

File Generation: Iterating through a list to generate and save CSV datasets to a hard drive.
Batch Rendering: Looping through a large dataset to generate and save dozens of visualizations
Database Writes: Adding rows or tables sequentially (slowly) into an external SQL database. Vectorization could cause the database to freeze.

title: Lecture 12
text:
for() loop or vectorize code?
3. Web Scraping and API Calls
Vectorizing a request (like trying to download from multiple websites in one pass) will get your IP address banned.

Set the pace: A for loop allows you to add a Sys.sleep(5) to pause between requests.
Error Handling: for allows you check and address errors in the middle of a large transaction (e.g., downloading specific pages). A vectorized function will crash and return an error with no feedback.

4. Severe Memory Constraints
Vectorization uses a lot of memory. If you are working with millions of rows on a machine with standard memory (like during DataFest), a complex vectorized operation might exceed memory and crash your R session. A for loop, operates on one chunk of data at a time. It will be slower, but uses fewer resources

Z score! A basic statistic seen in introductory stats courses.

Z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
\]

title: Lecture 12
text:
Programming Details

Once you have thought through some task like our “program a Z score”, pseudocode (usually 102A) might be helpful
Pseudocode serves as a bridge between human language and code. Use it to explain the logic of your code without going into the actual coding and its accompanying errors
Pseudocode for this example should start with some data, compute mean, compute standard deviation, compute Z scores.

title: Lecture 12
section: Pseudocode Example for Z score function
text:
Pseudocode Example for Z score function
Define a function named z_score that will accept a numeric vector (x) as input

Store the length of the numeric vector as n

Process the data:
    * compute the mean of the x values, use na.rm = TRUE
    * compute the standard deviation (which one?), use na.rm = TRUE
    * for each x value in the numeric vector, 
      + subtract the mean of x from this value
      + divide by the standard deviation of x
      + store the result in our created numeric vector
      + return the result

End

title: Lecture 12
section: Try applying the psuedocode logic to R
text:
Try applying the psuedocode logic to R

First get it to work, then improve it



Code
z_score <- function(x){
  # calculate a mean
  mean_x <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # calculate a standard deviation
  sd_x <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # calculate z score, store
  z <- (x - mean_x)/sd_x
  
  return(z) # you can use return if you want, no penalty
}

z_score(x)

title: Lecture 12
text:
vectors as index sets

We are not limited to numbers, any sequence can serve as an index
This is better presented as a .R file or in a notebook
Talk about the entire script and then work through the pieces
Steps

obtain a large data frame that could be subset in different ways
choose a variable suitable for subsetting, obtain a vector of unique values
create a list object to store all of the subsets (data frames), name each list component
create a folder (subdirectory) to hold our subsets
use the vector of names as the index set for our loop
populate our list object
also write each data frame as a .csv to our drive
check our results

title: Lecture 12
text:
entire code, not run

## I. Preparation
load("pokemon.RData") # any complex dataset will do, choose pokemon

type_names <- unique(pokemon_df$type_1) # extract the different types

pokemon_list <- vector("list", length = length(type_names)) 
# initialize a data structure to contain the separate data frames

names(pokemon_list) <- type_names # name each list component

# Create a dedicated folder so we don't clutter the main directory
# showWarnings = FALSE prevents an error if we run the script more than once
dir.create("pokemon_subsets", showWarnings = FALSE)

## II. For Loop 
for (current_type in seq_along(type_names)) {
  
  # 1. Populate our list
  pokemon_list[[current_type]] <- pokemon_df[pokemon_df$type_1 == type_names[current_type], ]
  
  # 2. Dynamically generate the file name (e.g., "Fire_pokemon.csv")
  file_name <- paste0(type_names[current_type], "_pokemon.csv")
  
  # 3. Safely construct the final path to our new folder
  # file.path() is essential because it automatically handles the correct 
  # slashes ( / vs \ ) depending on Mac or Windows.
  final_path <- file.path("pokemon_subsets", file_name)
  
  # 4. Write the csv files out to the hard drive
  write.csv(pokemon_list[[current_type]], file = final_path, row.names = FALSE)
}

## III. Checking it over

print("Export complete. Please check your project folder!")

title: Lecture 12
text:
The if

You may have seen examples, but let’s address it now.
R can evaluate conditional statements.
A conditional statement is a switch. The response it receives will determine which subsequent command to execute.
The if is THE conditional in R. Used much more than all the others. It’s format:

If (condition) {
     Statement_1
     Statement_2
     Etc
}

The condition is a logical expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.
The statements in the block {} will run only if the condition evaluates to TRUE.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Example

score <- 4
if (score == 5){ # FALSE
print("PERFECT") # this does not print
}
if (score <= 4){ # TRUE
print("Nice Try") # this will print
}

[1] "Nice Try"


A missing value (NA) for condition will throw an error.

if (score == log(-1)){ # NA or something else
print("You can't be less than zero") # will not run
}

Warning in log(-1): NaNs produced


Error in `if (score == log(-1)) ...`:
! missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

title: Lecture 12
Lecture 12
text:
Important note about if()

if() expects a single TRUE or FALSE, not a vector.
If you program something like:

if (is.na(c(NA, 1)))  

the if() will throw an error even though is.na(c(NA, 1)) correct
if (condition) runs the code only when the condition is TRUE.

title: Lecture 12
Lecture 12
Lecture 12
text:
(optional/102A) while()

A for() loop, repeats commands a fixed number of times
The while() loop is used when the number of iterations is unknown in advance
The while() loop repeats a set of commands as long as a specified condition is TRUE.

while (condition) {
# Commands go here
}
A while() loop is a repeating if statement:

The logical condition expression is evaluated.
If the condition is TRUE, the commands are executed.
Repeat steps 1 and 2 until the condition evaluates to FALSE, when the loop stops.

title: Lecture 12
text:
(optional/102A) While example
This will roll until a 12 is thrown

roll <- function() sample(1:6, 2, replace = TRUE) |> sum()

count <- 0
value <- 0

while (value != 12) {
  value <- roll()
  count <- count + 1
}

count

title: Lecture 12
text:
(optional/102A) Break

A break statement exits or “breaks” out of a loop.
A break is usually inside an if() statement so that the loop breaks when a certain condition is met (the exit condition).

if (condition) { # exit condition
break # stop and exit
}

(optional/102A) Next

A next is found in loops where we want to skip certain cases
But rare in everyday vectorized code.
A set of if could substitute


results <- c()

for (i in 1:100) {
  value <- sample(-5:5, 1)
  
  if (value <= 0) {
    next   # skip invalid values
  }
  
  results <- c(results, value)
}

title: Lecture 12
text:
Two pass

In some of the examples above, we used both replicate() and for() to solve the same problem
But sometimes you might hear an upper division instructor require a “Two-pass”
This means processing the data twice for accuracy — not just writing two different versions.
This is most important when rounding errors might be an issue

title: Lecture 12
text:
Two Pass Example: variance

It turns out that combinations of large values, small differences and rounding error can generates numerical instability so programming the variance like this


x <- c(1e12 + 1:10, 1e12 + 1:10)

# sample size
n <- length(x) 

# sample mean
x_bar <- mean(x) 

# compute the sum of squared deviations
ssd <- 0
for (i in seq_along(x)) {
ssd <- ssd + (x[i]- x_bar)^2
}

# compute the actual variance
variance_loop <- 1 / (n-1) * ssd

# a one pass variance
var_one_pass <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  (sum(x^2) - (sum(x)^2)/n) / (n - 1)
}

var_two_pass <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  mu <- mean(x)
  sum((x - mu)^2) / (n - 1)
}

c(var(x), variance_loop) # test

[1] 8.684211 8.684211

c(var(x), var_two_pass(x)) # test

[1] 8.684211 8.684211

c(var(x), var_one_pass(x)) # test - way off

[1] 8.684211e+00 2.260509e+08

all.equal(var(x), var_one_pass(x)) # test - way off

[1] "Mean relative difference: 26030104"

title: Lecture 12
text:
Scope

The body of the function creates its own (local) environment
Objects in the global environment are accessible within the function’s local environment.
But not all parts of all local objects are available in the global environment
Objects in the local environment take precedence over objects in the global environment. If an object within the function has the same name as one in the global environment, the local object will mask (cover) the global one, so the function will reference the local version only.

title: Lecture 12
text:
The … (ellipsis)

Some functions (e.g., data.frame) can accept any number of user specified-arguments.

The … (ellipsis) argument makes this possible.
… is often used when extending another function and the programmer does not want to copy the entire argument list of the original function.

Be cautious when using … If an argument is misspelled it will NOT generate an error. Also any arguments used after … must be fully named.

You can see whether an ellipsis is used in a function on the corresponding help page or with args().

title: Lecture 12
text:
Piping/Chaining

When writing complex program you will find yourself calling a function

on the output of another function
on the output of another function (repeated endlessly)
on the output of another function of an object.

Chaining (AKA piping) increases the readability of your code.
The output of the left-hand-side is used as the input for the first argument of the function specified on the right-hand-side.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Memory

Increasing the length of a vector element by element inside any loop (e.g., count <- c(count, value)) should generally be avoided.
Each time the vector grows by one element, R replaces the entire vector with a new vector in a new memory location that includes the additional element.
New memory space is allocated for each new vector, making this process time-consuming and inefficient.

Braun and Murdoch Solution: * Pre-allocate a vector of a fixed size for storage when possible to avoid this issue. * This will improve the performance of loops, especially when the number of iterations is large.

title: Lecture 12
text:
Argument Matching
Argument matching determines how R interprets function calls. There are different methods for this

ExactPartialPositionalMixedExample



For exact matching of arguments, each argument name (AKA tag) is written out fully to specify its value.
This method is the most error-free.

The order in which the arguments are given do not matter because they are named.

This method is most useful when a function has many possible arguments but we only use a few (like plot())
Unfortunately, this method requires more typing and more memorization.




Partial matching allows arguments to be used with an abbreviated name.
So less typing is involved and you can still write arguments in any order.

If your function has many arguments with similar abbreviations, this method will fail. (n= and name= as arguments don’t help)
Success here requires unique argument abbreviations




Positional Matching is when the argument names are not used and R interprets them based on their order.
This type of matching is best used with functions with few arguments.

Knowing the exact order/position of arguments is important here
I’m guilty of doing this — seq(1, 100, 2) instead of exact seq(from = 1, to = 100, by = 2)




exactly what it sounds like, using a mixture of the others



These will all run and give the same answer, some are more understandable than others

sd(ChickWeight$weight)
sd(ChickWeight$weight, na.rm = FALSE)
sd(ChickWeight$weight, na = FALSE)
sd(x = ChickWeight$weight)
sd(x = ChickWeight$weight, na.rm = FALSE)
sd(ChickWeight$weight, FALSE)
sd(na.rm = FALSE, x = ChickWeight$weight)
sd(na.rm = FALSE, ChickWeight$weight)

title: Lecture 12
text:
Some things worth mentioning

Indenting the body of the function is not required BUT highly recommended - especially if you plan to take 102A.
The output of the last command in the body is the output of the function.
If the last command does not have an output nothing will be returned
R does have a return() statement that is optional. An R function with a return() will output whatever you specify and then immediately exit/end the function.
A function can only return one object. To return multiple objects, store them in a list.
if() expects exactly one TRUE or FALSE
= means “assignment” and == means “comparison”
is.na() and !is.na() can be useful

text:
Subsetting a subset
This can look daunting, we are taking a subset of one variable given the values on a different variable in the last example on the previous slide.

table(EQ2025$QUALITY[EQ2025$MAG > 3]) 
# compare EQ2025[EQ2025$MAG > 3, ] from above or EQ2025[EQ2025$MAG > 3, "QUALITY" ] or EQ2025[EQ2025$MAG > 3, 10 ]

This is where the “then” operator (|>) helps, we extract the exact subset we want and then table() the subset. The code is easier to read.

EQ2025$QUALITY[EQ2025$MAG > 3] |> table()


R does not look inside your data frame, you must explicitly reference columns (e.g., EQ2025$MAG) on the row side of [r, c]
The second argument (columns) must be column indices or names, not the actual values of a column.

Braun & Murdoch Chapter 2.4.1

Recall the Earthquake data. Suppose you were told to create a subset of data where the magnitude (MAG) must be at least 2.5 and the quality (QUALITY) must be “A”.
How would you write the request?


# this works but is horribly inefficient
# you don't want to be occupying so much of your resources

MAG25 <- EQ2025[EQ2025$MAG >= 2.5, ]
ANDQUALITYA <- MAG25[MAG25$QUALITY == "A",]


Let’s spend a little time with the Boolean Algebra of R
Wikipedia tells us: Introduced by George Boole, it uses operators like AND, OR, and NOT to model, analyze, and simplify logical expressions, forming the fundamental basis of digital circuit design and computer programming

title: Lecture 10
text:
A Truth Table

The body of this table shows how logical operations behave for every possible combination of TRUE and FALSE.




Chapter 2.4.1 Truth Table


Row 1 – A = TRUE, B = TRUE.
Results:
not A → FALSE
not B → FALSE
A and B → TRUE (both are TRUE)
A or B → TRUE (at least one is TRUE)

title: Lecture 10
text:
Short version

NOT (!) flips TRUE FALSE
AND (&) TRUE only when both are TRUE
OR (|) TRUE when at least one is TRUE

title: Lecture 10
text:
Factors - What they do

Factors are variables in R which take on a limited number of different values, typically these variables represent non-numerical or “categorical” information.

We use factors in statistical modeling because non-numerical variables (e.g., genre — rap, rock, pop, electronic) enter into statistical models differently than numerical variables (one-hot encoding, indicator, dummy coding)

Designating non-numerical data as factors insures that the more advanced model estimation functions (101ABC) in R will treat these types of variables correctly.

Factors will also let us order a “categorical” value in any way we wish, not only alphabetically. This is also useful when modeling.

title: Lecture 10
text:
Dates & Times

Frequently ignored but ever present and often quite useful
If not told otherwise, R will read data containing dates as we understand them as Character (or worse, Factor)
Dates (there are exceptions) are stored by R as the number of days or seconds from January 1, 1970, using negative numbers for date before January 1, 1970.
The default format expected by R is a four digit year, followed by a month, then a day, separated by either dashes or slashes.
The base R as.Date() function converts character representations of dates (without times, e.g. 1/1/2020)
The base R strptime() function converts character representations of dates and times to Unix (POSIX) time. This is used when data has times, time zones, AM/PM time stamps, etc.

title: Lecture 10
text:
Rules of Thumb

The general rule for date/time data in R is to use the simplest technique possible.
as.Date( ) will usually be the best choice because dates typically appear without times. Examples might be trading date, historical dates, birth date. The example from earlier on deaths in the workplace gives dates but not time.
strptime( ) would usually be used if there is also a timestamp associated with the date. Generally, data generated by computer, such as a system date, will have a timestamp.
there are additional base R functiona such as

as.POSIXlt() - generates a LIST of components (good for extraction like day of the week).
as.POSIXct() - generates a numeric timestamp (good for computation)

title: Lecture 10
text:
Examples
The unclass function is only being used to reveal R’s storage of the date (never will ask you about it):

unclass(as.Date("1969-12-30")) 

[1] -2

unclass(as.Date("1969/12/31")) 

[1] -1

unclass(as.Date("1970/1/1")) # day zero

[1] 0

unclass(as.Date("1970-1-2"))

[1] 1

unclass(as.Date("1970/01/03"))

[1] 2

Sys.Date() # current date 

[1] "2026-04-30"

class(Sys.Date())

[1] "Date"

unclass(Sys.Date())  # how R stores it

Understanding R’s Graphic System

R has a (1) traditional graphics system and also (2) a grid graphics system
The most popular visualization package in R is ggplot2 which is a graphics system that is an implementation of the grid graphics system. (next lecture)

title: Lecture 07
section: The Logic of Constructing Plots in R
text:
The Logic of Constructing Plots in R

The functions on the previous slide could be roughly categorized in “high level” and “low level” functions.
A plot is created in base R graphics by first calling a high-level function.
A high-level graphics function can create a plot and does not require any other function to precede it
A low-level graphics function are called to add more output to the plot (such as additional lines or points). These functions depend on a previous high-level function.
Plots created in base R are layered like a cake. We initialize a plot with a high level function and then layer it with additional information provided by low level functions

title: Lecture 07
text:
Rough Categorization








Category
Purpose
Examples




High-Level
Bottom Layer of the “cake”
plot(), hist(), boxplot(), barplot(), heatmap(), pairs(), persp(), contour(), smoothScatter()


Low-Level
Added “cake” layers
points(), lines(), abline(), text(), legend(), axis(), title(), segments(), rug()

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot()

The most important high-level plotting function in base R graphics is plot( )
plot can be used to create simple scatter plots( ) (among other things)
plot( ) can take many arguments allowing for extreme customization.
The first argument to plot( ) is data, usually a vector, but it could be a data frame. plot() will behave differently depending on the data
The second argument can usually be anything…

title: Lecture 07
text:
two specific vectors from many

You must specify them, x first, then y (unless you use argument names x= and y=). Extraction is an important skill. All 3 lines below will give exactly the same plot:


op <- par()
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, main = "No argument names") 
# works but bad for communication

plot(x = iris$Sepal.Length, y = iris$Sepal.Width, main = "Argument names") 
# 102 happy place, named and in order

plot(y = iris$Sepal.Width, x = iris$Sepal.Length, main = "Argument names, any order") 
# always clear when you use argument naming

par(op)


You will see par() after the break, here I am copying the existing, then modifying a default from one plot per images to 2 by 2 or 4 images then restoring the original.

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot() help - description and usage
help(plot)

The Default Scatterplot Function

Description:

     Draw a scatter plot with decorations such as axes and titles in
     the active graphics window.

Usage:

     ## Default S3 method:
     plot(x, y = NULL, type = "p",  xlim = NULL, ylim = NULL,
          log = "", main = NULL, sub = NULL, xlab = NULL, ylab = NULL,
          ann = par("ann"), axes = TRUE, frame.plot = axes,
          panel.first = NULL, panel.last = NULL, asp = NA,
          xgap.axis = NA, ygap.axis = NA,
          ...)
The ... suggests even more potential options not fully documented. So if you include an argument that plot() does recognize, it passes it along to associated other functions. Problem is, R doesn’t necessarily tell you if it’s completely unrecognized, things just don’t happen.

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot() help - arguments
Arguments:

    x, y: the ‘x’ and ‘y’ arguments provide the x and y coordinates for
          the plot.  Any reasonable way of defining the coordinates is
          acceptable.  See the function ‘xy.coords’ for details.  If
          supplied separately, they must be of the same length.

    type: 1-character string giving the type of plot desired.  The
          following values are possible, for details, see ‘plot’: ‘"p"’
          for points, ‘"l"’ for lines, ‘"b"’ for both points and lines,
          ‘"c"’ for empty points joined by lines, ‘"o"’ for overplotted
          points and lines, ‘"s"’ and ‘"S"’ for stair steps and ‘"h"’
          for histogram-like vertical lines.  Finally, ‘"n"’ does not
          produce any points or lines.

    xlim: the x limits (x1, x2) of the plot.  Note that ‘x1 > x2’ is
          allowed and leads to a ‘reversed axis’.

          The default value, ‘NULL’, indicates that the range of the
          finite values to be plotted should be used.

    ylim: the y limits of the plot.

     log: a character string which contains ‘"x"’ if the x axis is to
          be logarithmic, ‘"y"’ if the y axis is to be logarithmic and
          ‘"xy"’ or ‘"yx"’ if both axes are to be logarithmic.

    main: a main title for the plot, see also ‘title’.

     sub: a subtitle for the plot.

    xlab: a label for the x axis, defaults to a description of ‘x’.

    ylab: a label for the y axis, defaults to a description of ‘y’.

     ann: a logical value indicating whether the default annotation
          (title and x and y axis labels) should appear on the plot.

    axes: a logical value indicating whether both axes should be drawn
          on the plot.  Use graphical parameter ‘"xaxt"’ or ‘"yaxt"’ to
          suppress just one of the axes.

frame.plot: a logical indicating whether a box should be drawn around
          the plot.

panel.first: an ‘expression’ to be evaluated after the plot axes are
          set up but before any plotting takes place.  This can be
          useful for drawing background grids or scatterplot smooths.
          Note that this works by lazy evaluation: passing this
          argument from other ‘plot’ methods may well not work since it
          may be evaluated too early.

panel.last: an expression to be evaluated after plotting has taken
          place but before the axes, title and box are added.  See the
          comments about ‘panel.first’.

     asp: the y/x aspect ratio, see ‘plot.window’.
     xgap.axis, ygap.axis: the x/y axis gap factors, passed as ‘gap.axis’ to
          the two ‘axis()’ calls (when ‘axes’ is true, as per default).

     ...: other graphical parameters (see ‘par’ and section ‘Details’
          below).

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot() help - details
Details:

     Commonly used graphical parameters are:

     ‘col’ The colors for lines and points.  Multiple colors can be
          specified so that each point can be given its own color.  If
          there are fewer colors than points they are recycled in the
          standard fashion.  Lines will all be plotted in the first
          colour specified.

     ‘bg’ a vector of background colors for open plot symbols, see
          ‘points’.  Note: this is *not* the same setting as
          ‘par("bg")’.

     ‘pch’ a vector of plotting characters or symbols: see ‘points’.

     ‘cex’ a numerical vector giving the amount by which plotting
          characters and symbols should be scaled relative to the
          default.  This works as a multiple of ‘par("cex")’.  ‘NULL’
          and ‘NA’ are equivalent to ‘1.0’.  Note that this does not
          affect annotation: see below.

     ‘lty’ a vector of line types, see ‘par’.

     ‘cex.main’, ‘col.lab’, ‘font.sub’, etc settings for main- and
          sub-title and axis annotation, see ‘title’ and ‘par’.

     ‘lwd’ a vector of line widths, see ‘par’.

Note

The previous slide revealed (using par( ) - the unlist function converted the resulting list into a vector so that it would fit on a single page) - it revealed all of the graphical parameters (defaults) in place when I was creating my plots.
These control parameters such as the color, whether the axes are on a logarithmic scale, etc.
This part of the lecture is all about customizing our plots via the graphical parameters. There are over 100 parameters, we will examine a few: colors, symbols, lines, and text.

title: Lecture 07
text:
At Minimum
Thinking ahead to project 3

Visualizations that might impress a potential employer/manager/etc.
Descriptive Title: A title that highlights the main message rather than just “X vs Y”.
Axis Titles/Labels: Descriptive labeling for both axes (what are we looking at?)
Units of Measurement: If used, should appear somewhere
Legends: When colors or shapes need distinguishing
Legible Text: 10-point font size is about as small as most will accept
Data Source and other annotations: Try to give credit where credit is due
Source: Biorender

title: Lecture 07
text:
Colors

R has 657 built-in colors, (see colors() )many more can be created using other libraries. These are colors R recognizes by name.
There are 3 basic settings used in base R graphics: col=, fg= and bg=

col= is used for the colors of lines, symbols and text
fg= specifies the colors of axes and borders
bg= specifies the color of the background or fill

There are several specific settings such as col.main= for the plot title, col.axis = for the axis labels etc.
You can specify colors by name, by hexadecimal code, and by number.
You can find color specifications everywhere and generate a version that R can use example: UCLA Colors
You can find websites to help you choose specific colors

title: Lecture 07
text:
Applying colors
In plot, the col= option will work and it can accept vectors of colors too.

plot(
    Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length,
    data = iris, 
    main = "An Iris Plot",
    sub = "Sepal Width on Sepal.Length",
    xlab = "Sepal Length",
    ylab = "Sepal Width",
    pch = 19, # change default symbol
    col = c(UCLAB, UCLAG) # use both colors or use Hex "#2774AE", "#FFD100"
  )

pch = will change the default symbol. Try ?pch at the console prompt to see all of the possibilities.

title: Lecture 07
text:
Adding and modifying lines

lty= controls the linetype, from the documentation:
1-character string giving the type of plot desired. The following values are possible, for details, see plot:

“p” for points,
“l” for lines,
“b” for both points and lines,
“c” for empty points joined by lines,
“o” for overplotted points and lines,
“s” and “S” for stair steps and
“h” for histogram-like vertical lines.


Finally, “n” does not produce any points or lines.

lwd= controls the line width, so lwd= 2 means twice the default thickness
See ?plot.default for a deeper dive

title: Lecture 07
text:
Example

This is a financial data package and we will use it to generate multiple lines to plot.


#install.packages("quantmod")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(quantmod))

# Fetch data for the last 90 days 
getFX("EUR/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90) # Sys.Date() is today's date
getFX("GBP/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)
getFX("CHF/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)
getFX("CAD/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)

# Merge them into one dataset for plotting
currency_data <- merge(EURUSD, GBPUSD, CHFUSD, CADUSD)
# head(currency_data) # always check

# multiple lines
plot(x = index(currency_data),  # index values, dates here
     y = currency_data[,1],   # first currency
     ylim = range(currency_data), # makes sure the y-axis is large enough to accommodate the possible values
     type = "l",  # line type - solid
     lwd= 1.5,   # line thickness, 1.5 times default
     main="Currency Trends (Last 2 Months) vs USD", 
     col="blue", 
     ylab="Exchange Rate")
# we add "low-level" graphical functions, lines()
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,2], col="red", lwd= 1.5)
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,3], col="green", lwd= 1.5)
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,4], col="magenta", lwd= 1.5)
legend("right", legend=c("EUR", "GBP", "CHF", "CAD"), 
       col=c("blue", "red", "green", "magenta"), lty= 1, lwd= 1.5, cex= 0.6)

but legend can accept:

title: Lecture 07
text:
filtering in base R

An important skill and when we examine the Tidyverse, you can judge
Let’s suppose we think ‘we will drop the least popular’
In base R filtering means:


Keep rows where a condition is TRUE.

Everything comes back to this fundamental pattern:
df[ some_condition , ]

read “we have a dataframe (df) extract some_condition is TRUE all the columns”

title: Lecture 07
text:
Application

Suppose we want to keep those tracks which have a popularity of at least 1 because we noticed about 10% of songs had a popularity of zero.
Our condition translated into R, looks like

spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1
or
spotify_songs$track_popularity > 0

Unfortunately, if you only ran this, R would return a vector with as many rows as spotify_songs but full of TRUE and FALSE (try it, you’ll see)
BUT when we insert it into a dataframe extract:

spotify_songs[spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1, ]

R will respond by keeping only those rows for which this condition is true and give us the filtered data frame that we want to use.

title: Lecture 07
text:
Make it real

# our conditioning variable
fivenum(spotify_songs$track_popularity)

[1]   0  24  45  62 100

# filter with a condition
spotify_filtered <- spotify_songs[spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1, ]

# always check
fivenum(spotify_filtered$track_popularity)

[1]   1  31  48  63 100



Now plot it


plot(x = spotify_filtered$duration_ms, y = spotify_filtered$track_popularity,
     main = "Filtered and possibly more useless than ever")

smoothScatter() turns a scatterplot into a color map that shows where points are most concentrated
This is useful when you have so many data points, it is difficult to see anything useful in your scatterplot.


rgb.palette <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "orange", "red"), space = "rgb")
smoothScatter(x = spotify_filtered$duration_ms, 
              y = spotify_filtered$track_popularity, 
              colramp = rgb.palette,
              main = "But patterns may begin to emerge")

title: Lecture 07

Barplot is “not smart”

barplot() will not do math for you, so your data must be in totals (or tabled)
if it is a vector (one-way table), each value will be a bar
if it is a matrix (two-way table), each column will be bar


# Each value gets a bar and a color
my_vector <- c(A = 10, B = 20, c = 30)
barplot(my_vector, col = c("red", "yellow", "dodgerblue"))

title: Lecture 07
text:
Matrix example

The assumption is that the numerical values are some type of total or count value
Matrices need to be convert to a two-way table to be plotted here


op <- par() # store the defaults, turn your warnings off
par(mfrow = c(1,2)) # change the plot window appearance
matrix(seq(10, 60, by= 10), nrow = 2) |> as.table() |> barplot(col = c("red", "dodgerblue"), main = "2x3 matrix")
matrix(seq(10, 60, by= 10), nrow = 3) |> as.table() |> barplot(col = c("red", "dodgerblue", "yellow"), main = "3x2 matrix")







par(op) # restore the original

title: Lecture 07
text:
Aside: table()

The table() function is ancient but easy and useful. Especially when trying to build data for plots
from the documentation, simplified

table(...,
      exclude = if (useNA == "no") c(NA, NaN),
      useNA = c("no", "ifany", "always"),
      dnn = list.names(...), deparse.level = 1)

...        one or more objects which can be interpreted as factors (including numbers or character strings), or a list (such as a data frame) whose components can be so interpreted. 
exclude  levels to remove for all factors in .... If it does not contain NA and useNA is not specified, it implies useNA = "ifany". 

it needs to be demo’ed, then you are quite clever and can build on the basics
I would recommend always setting useNA = "always" until you know there are no NA in your data or have dealt with them.

We can draw better and more flexible heatmaps using other packages but base R has one and if you haven’t seen one before, here is your introduction.

title: Lecture 07
text: Heatmap result

title: Lecture 07
text:
Takeaway for the Heatmap

A heat map is a just tool like the others tools
It is a scaled matrix of numerical values represented by colors
They represent Z-scores (standard deviations from the mean of the column)
A “Hot” color (here, Yellow): This value is high relative to other values.
A “Cold” color (here deep Purple): This value is low relative to the other.

title: Lecture 07
text:
Histogram Characteristics

Designed for Continuous Data – esp. data measured on a scale, such as height, weight, age etc.
Histograms generally have no gaps between bars (compare boxplot)
Used to identify the shape of data (e.g., symmetry or skewness), central tendency, and spread.
Can be used for outlier detection - gaps or unusual data points

title: Lecture 07
text:
hist() for histograms



help(hist)

title: Lecture 07
text:
basic example

pokemon_df$BMI <- pokemon_df$weight / (pokemon_df$height)^2
hist(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id < 3])

title: Lecture 07
text:
common options

add titles and labels, change color, change to density


hist(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id < 3], prob = TRUE, col = "cyan", 
     xlab = "BMI", main = "Histogram of Pokemon BMI")

title: Lecture 07
text:
additional options

adjust the number of breaks (cells), adjust the height of the y-axis, add lines and legend


hist(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id < 3], prob = TRUE, col = "cyan", 
     xlab = "BMI", main = "Histogram of Pokemon BMI", breaks = 20, ylim = c(0, 0.03))
# Add density curve
density_curve <- density(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id < 3],
                       na.rm = TRUE) # Remove NA values if any
lines(density_curve, col = "red", lwd = 2) # Add density to plot

# Calculate median BMI for each generation
median_bmi01 <- median(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id == 1], 
     na.rm = TRUE)
median_bmi02 <- median(pokemon_df$BMI[pokemon_df$generation_id == 2], 
     na.rm = TRUE)

# Add vertical line for median BMIs for gen1 and gen2
abline(v = median_bmi01, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2) 
# Add vertical line with blue color, width 2, and dashed line type
abline(v = median_bmi02, col = "magenta", lwd = 2, lty = 2) 
# Add vertical line with magenta color, width 2, and dashed line type

# Add legend with location, text, specified colors and line types
legend("topright", 
       legend = c("Density Curve", "Median BMI Gen 1", "Median BMI Gen 2"), 
       col = c("red", "blue", "magenta"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2, 2))

title: Lecture 07
text:
image, persp, contour

image() displays data as a image, contour() as lines of equal height, and persp() as a 3D surface. All using the same data in a panel display


# Save current graphical settings
op <- par()

# Layout: 1 row, 3 columns
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2), oma = c(0, 0, 2, 0))

# Image (heatmap-style)
image(
  volcano,
  col = terrain.colors(20),
  main = "image(volcano)",
  xlab = "X",
  ylab = "Y"
)

# Contour
contour(
  volcano,
  col = "darkgreen",
  lwd = 1.2,
  main = "contour(volcano)",
  xlab = "X",
  ylab = "Y"
)

# Perspective (3D)
persp(
  volcano,
  theta = 40,
  phi = 20,
  expand = 0.6,
  col = "tan",
  shade = 0.5,
  border = "gray",
  main = "persp(volcano)"
)

# Overall title
mtext("Three Views of the Same Data (volcano matrix)", outer = TRUE)

# Restore settings
par(op)

A Data Science Workflow







From Google




From CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network):

R is a system for statistical computation and graphics. It consists of a language plus a run-time environment with graphics, a debugger, access to certain system functions, and the ability to run programs stored in script files.

Translation:

R is a language with an interpreter and a standard library (toolkit/toolbox of functions)
With execution support code (behind the scenes code that helps your R code run on your computer)
All for the practice of statistics (involves computation,simulation, data visualization etc.)

R can also monitor/analyze code, identify coding errors, interact with your operating system, run programs saved on your computer as scripts (or similar) among other things.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “Take this data, then filter it, then group it, then summarize the mean, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how the code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveals the truth in the data.

R v Python Example 1
Let’s look at a bivariate regression: one Y (dependent), one X (independent)

RPythonTakeaways


If you already have R running on your computer, you can try this

model1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

summary(model1)


Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.5432 -2.3647 -0.1252  1.4096  6.8727 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  37.2851     1.8776  19.858  < 2e-16 ***
wt           -5.3445     0.5591  -9.559 1.29e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 3.046 on 30 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7528,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7446 
F-statistic: 91.38 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 1.294e-10








R has “built-in” data, Python does not (mtcars)
Notice the “<-” in R this is called a “gets”, it is used for assignment.read it “model 1 gets”
Python uses “=” for assignment and options
You can use “=” for assignment in R, but it is really meant to identify options
R is written comparable to way we think about things in statistics lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars) lm is the basic linear model (lm) FUNCTION (important word) and the () encloses its “arguments”. Functions do all of the “work” in R.
~ means “as a function of” so linear model - mpg as a function of wt the data is mtcars
You don’t need to print() explicitly in R, you must in Python to see results

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, it is treated like how the computer wants its input formatted.

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) is a function of \(x\).” R automatically handles things like creating “dummy variables” for categorical information (e.g., turning “Species” into 0s and 1s) and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. You then “One-Hot Encode” your categories and strip away the column names, then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

R can also monitor/analyze code, identify coding errors, interact with your operating system, run programs saved on your computer as scripts (or similar) among other things.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Activity #1 Takeaways

In the beginning, R is like a calculator
Numbers, operators, vectors, data frames, functions are objects.

A simplification: virtually everything in R is an object.
Names like x, y, z, iris, rivers are associated with R objects and by calling the name, we have access to the associated object
The fundamental data structure in R is the vector
Vectors are indexed (elements are numbered 1 to however many elements we have)

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “I want to study something which involves data, get the data, then filter/subset it, then group it, then summarize/describe, then model, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how your programming code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveal the truth found in the data.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, a statistical model is treated like “how does the computer wants its input formatted?”

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) changes in response to \(x\).” R automatically handles things creating the underlying matrix and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries(toolkits) require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. Then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

title: Lecture 01
text:
R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

print(result)


Python pandas is still readable even when complex
import pandas as pd

result = df[df["year"] > 2020].groupby("state")["y"].mean().reset_index(name="mean_yield")

title: Lecture 01
text:
Where are we?

Learn how to be a “System Architect” – someone who understands how code (regardless of the specific language) serves a specific business or research goal (this AI cannot do yet). Study/ understand the process in addition to trusting it.
Focus on possessing AI Augmentation Skills – where AI is used as a tool to help humans do more, rather than replace humans. When coding in this class, AI is your helper to develop your computational thinking and broaden your understanding of the application of the code beyond the problem in front of us.
AI is the best at “book learning” (explicit knowledge) so instead of competing – leverage AI to help you gain practical, hands-on experience through projects and then internships and then jobs. Show that you can apply what you have learned in the areas/industries/fields that you want to join.
Develop your “Tacit Knowledge” – an advanced form of pattern recognition that the brain does subconsciously after years of experience - having good judgment arising from “the feel” of a situation, for example - handling complex client interactions, dealing with “messiness” (when things do not go as planned). Develop your Spidey Senses for a situation.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The Value of Computational Thinking



Decomposition - Breaking a larger problem down into smaller pieces
Pattern Recognition - Looking for similarities within and across problems
Abstraction - Avoid hyperfocusing on granular details and focusing instead on developing general solutions
Algorithm Design - Automating the process efficiently, ensuring reproducibility and reducing the need for excessive human intervention





Image created by ISTE & CSTA

title: Lecture 01
text:
Decomposition

Basic StructureAnd Still More


By the end of the quarter, instead of simply saying “I analyzed some data,” we can articulate more of what is involved as we learn how to do decompose what we do while learn R:

I read some data
I prepared the data for analysis
I generated statistics and visualizations
I modeled outcomes
I communicated my findings to others



and learn a little about a complete/professional workflow:

Ingest data (read CSV / JSON / SQL database)
Clean & make data consistent (e.g. fix various date formats)
Address missing values
Recode categories (regroup/relabel values)
Transform values (logarithms, standardization)
Engineer new variables (great creative skills)
Aggregate or Reshape/restructure data
Model / analyze the cleaned data
Validate/verify/reproduce results
Communicate results (tables, figures, reports)
Return to previous steps to refine one’s understanding (iterative)

Each step is clear and repeatable across different data & problems

title: Lecture 01
text:
Pattern Recognition
Intuitively seeking structure, repetition, regularity in data:

noticing the same data-cleaning steps apply to many different types of data files
recognizing that bootstrapping, permutation tests, and cross-validation share a common resampling pattern (upper division)
seeing that multiple models differ only by a formula or parameter

This is where the need for loops, reusable functions, and pipelines (making raw data analyzable) arise.
If I have time, the streetwise soldier who intuition saved his platoon during the worst of the Vietnam War (1965-1973).

title: Lecture 01
text:
Abstraction
Focus on what matters, minimize what does not:

data is “rows = cases, columns = variables” rather than obsessing over file format
thinking in terms of distributions rather than individual observations
defining a function that works for “any dataset”

Abstraction is what helps you generalize from one analysis to the next. This helps maximize productivity and minimize time spent in repetitive tasks.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Algorithmic thinking, good design
Create a clear, step-by-step procedure that produces a (reproducible) result

an iterative fitting routine
simulation steps (“repeat 10,000 times…”)
a reproducible analysis script that always gives the same output from the same input

This is the bridge between statistical reasoning and actual computation.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why do this?
The American Statistical Association emphasizes computational thinking because modern statistics is no longer just formulas on paper:

Simulation > closed-form solutions (formulas)
Resampling (let the data tell us) > asymptotics (trust the math)
Reproducible pipelines > one time calculations/analyses
Data wrangling > textbook-clean datasets

statistical thinking + computational thinking = data science.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Workflow in Action & computational thinking

Decomposition is like the flow of data and thought from problem to solution
Pattern recognition is like seeing that flow across different projects
Abstraction is like “cleaning” & “modeling” & “reporting” generally
Algorithmic thinking is about having ordered, executable steps

Computational Thinking forces us to stop thinking in terms of isolated/one-off projects and start thinking in terms reproducible processes and the enterprise (whatever it may be) as a whole

# 2. Setup Figure

# 4. Label the Top 3 Outliers

top_3_idx = np.abs(model.resid).sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).index

for i in top_3_idx:
    ax.annotate(i, (model.fittedvalues[i], model.resid[i]),

title: Lecture 13
text:
The if

You may have seen examples, but let’s address it now.
R can evaluate conditional statements.
A conditional statement is a switch. The response it receives will determine which subsequent command to execute.
The if is THE conditional in R. Used much more than all the others. It’s format:

If (condition) {
     Statement_1
     Statement_2
     Etc
}

The condition is a logical expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE (and nothing else).
The statements in the block {} will run only if the condition evaluates to TRUE.
R is not too particular about indentation, other languages are.

title: Lecture 13
text:
Examples

score <- 5
if (score == 5){ # FALSE
  print("PERFECT") # this does not print
}

[1] "PERFECT"

if (score <= 4){ # TRUE
  print("Good Try") # this will print
}
# Multiple if statements are independent. The two above are coded to be mutually exclusive so its OK
# Try changing the second one to score <= 5, you'll get both...

A missing value (NA) for condition will throw an error.

if (score == log(-1)){ # NA or something else
  print("You can't be less than zero") # will not run
}

Warning in log(-1): NaNs produced


Error in `if (score == log(-1)) ...`:
! missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed


To cover NA conditions one could

score <- NA
if (is.na(score)){ # evaluates to TRUE or FALSE
  print("Score is missing") 
}

[1] "Score is missing"

title: Lecture 13
Lecture 13
text:
Important note about if()

if() expects a single TRUE or FALSE, not a vector.
If you program something like:

if (is.na(c(NA, 1)))  

the if() will throw an error even though is.na(c(NA, 1)) correct
if (condition) runs the code only when the condition is TRUE.
if you have a vector, you will need a loop, this one is silly, but it works


x <- 1:10

for (i in x) {
  if (i %% 2 == 0) {
    print(paste(i, "is even"))
  }
}

[1] "2 is even"
[1] "4 is even"
[1] "6 is even"
[1] "8 is even"
[1] "10 is even"

# you could have written it paste(x[x %% 2 == 0], "is even")

vectorized ifelse()

ifelse() works great when you have two possible outcomes


actuarial_results <- c(71, 91, 69, 88, 93, 72)
ifelse(actuarial_results >=70, "PASSED", "FAILED")

         ifelse(scores >= 90, "A",

title: Lecture 13
Lecture 13
text:
(optional/102A) while()

A for() loop, repeats commands a fixed number of times
The while() loop is used when the number of iterations is unknown in advance
The while() loop repeats a set of commands as long as a specified condition is TRUE.

while (condition) {
# Commands go here
}
A while() loop is a repeating if statement:

The logical condition expression is evaluated.
If the condition is TRUE, the commands are executed.
Repeat steps 1 and 2 until the condition evaluates to FALSE, when the loop stops.


Best used when the stopping condition is open-ended (alternative is a for and a break)
Like modeling processes that change until a certain level or value is reached (converges)

title: Lecture 13
text:
(optional/102A) While example

This will roll until a 12 is thrown


roll <- function() sample(1:6, 2, replace = TRUE) |> sum()

count <- 0
value <- 0

while (value != 12) {
  value <- roll()
  count <- count + 1
}

count

[1] 10



you might try running the while several times to see the count change
you could save the results of course and plot them etc.

title: Lecture 13
text:
(optional/102A) While example
Here is a way to use an &&

roll <- function() sample(1:6, 2, replace = TRUE) |> sum()

count <- 0
value <- 0

while (value != 12 && count < 100) { # don't let it run too long
  value <- roll()
  count <- count + 1
}

count

[1] 87



again, you could run this countless times and if you got a result of 100, the loop stopped
the result would be some kind of cap on the possibilities

title: Lecture 13
text:
(optional/102A) Break

A break statement exits or “breaks” out of a loop.
A break is usually inside an if() statement so that the loop breaks when a certain condition is met (the exit condition).
This is often used to rewrite a “while” as long as you have some kind of limit (e.g., 100)

if (condition) { # exit condition
break # stop and exit
}

title: Lecture 13
Lecture 13
Lecture 13
text:
Two pass

In some of the examples in this and the previous lecture, we used both replicate() and for() to solve the same problem
But sometimes you might hear an upper division instructor require a “Two-pass”
This means processing the data twice for accuracy — not just writing two different versions.
This is most important when rounding errors might be an issue

title: Lecture 13
text:
Two Pass Example: variance

It turns out that combinations of large values, small differences and rounding error can generates numerical instability so programming the variance like this


x <- c(1e12 + 1:10, 1e12 + 1:10)

# sample size
n <- length(x) 

# sample mean
x_bar <- mean(x) 

# compute the sum of squared deviations
ssd <- 0
for (i in seq_along(x)) {
ssd <- ssd + (x[i]- x_bar)^2
}

# compute the actual variance
variance_loop <- 1 / (n-1) * ssd

# a one pass variance
var_one_pass <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  (sum(x^2) - (sum(x)^2)/n) / (n - 1)
}

var_two_pass <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  mu <- mean(x)
  sum((x - mu)^2) / (n - 1)
}

c(var(x), variance_loop) # test

[1] 8.684211 8.684211

c(var(x), var_two_pass(x)) # test

[1] 8.684211 8.684211

c(var(x), var_one_pass(x)) # test - way off

[1] 8.684211e+00 2.260509e+08

all.equal(var(x), var_one_pass(x)) # test - way off

[1] "Mean relative difference: 26030104"

title: Lecture 13
text:
Scope (where mistakes happen)

The body of the function creates its own (local) environment
Objects in the global environment are accessible within the function’s local environment.
But not all parts of all local objects are available in the global environment
Objects in the local environment take precedence over objects in the global environment.
If an object within the function has the same name as one in the global environment, the local object will mask (cover) the global one, so the function will reference the local version only.

title: Lecture 13
text:
The … (ellipsis)

Some functions (e.g., data.frame) can accept any number of user specified-arguments.

The … (ellipsis) argument makes this possible.
… is often used when extending another function and the programmer does not want to copy the entire argument list of the original function.

Be cautious when using … If an argument is misspelled it will NOT generate an error. Also any arguments used after … must be fully named.

You can see whether an ellipsis is used in a function on the corresponding help page or with args().

title: Lecture 13
text:
Piping/Chaining

When writing complex program you will find yourself calling a function

on the output of another function
on the output of another function (repeated endlessly)
on the output of another function of an object.

Chaining (AKA piping) increases the readability of your code.
The output of the left-hand-side is used as the input for the first argument of the function specified on the right-hand-side.

title: Lecture 13
text:
Memory

Increasing the length of a vector element by element inside any loop (e.g., count <- c(count, value)) should generally be avoided.
Each time the vector grows by one element, R replaces the entire vector with a new vector in a new memory location that includes the additional element.
New memory space is allocated for each new vector, making this process time-consuming and inefficient.

Braun and Murdoch Solution: * Pre-allocate a vector of a fixed size for storage when possible to avoid this issue. * This will improve the performance of loops, especially when the number of iterations is large.

title: Lecture 13
text:
Some helpful functions
Used to explain functions

formals(sd) # arguments - wants a vector, na.rm = FALSE by default

$x


$na.rm
[1] FALSE



body(sd) # body of the function, sd is the sqrt of variance

sqrt(var(if (is.vector(x) || is.factor(x)) x else as.double(x), 
    na.rm = na.rm))



environment(sd) # basically where it resides

<environment: namespace:stats>

title: Lecture 13
text:
Argument Matching
Argument matching determines how R interprets function calls. There are different methods for this

ExactPartialPositionalMixedExample



For exact matching of arguments, each argument name (AKA tag) is written out fully to specify its value.
This method is the most error-free.

The order in which the arguments are given do not matter because they are named.

This method is most useful when a function has many possible arguments but we only use a few (like plot())
Unfortunately, this method requires more typing and more memorization.




Partial matching allows arguments to be used with an abbreviated name.
So less typing is involved and you can still write arguments in any order.

If your function has many arguments with similar abbreviations, this method will fail. (n= and name= as arguments don’t help)
Success here requires unique argument abbreviations




Positional Matching is when the argument names are not used and R interprets them based on their order.
This type of matching is best used with functions with few arguments.

Knowing the exact order/position of arguments is important here
I’m guilty of doing this — seq(1, 100, 2) instead of exact seq(from = 1, to = 100, by = 2)




exactly what it sounds like, using a mixture of the others



These will all run and give the same answer, some are more understandable than others

title: Lecture 13
text:
Some things worth mentioning

Indenting the body of the function is not required in R BUT highly recommended - especially if you plan to take 102A or learn Python.
The output of the last command in the body is the output of the function.
If the last command does not have an output nothing will be returned
R does have a return() statement that is optional. An R function with a return() will output whatever you specify and then immediately exit/end the function.
A function can only return one object. To return multiple objects, store them in a list.
if() expects exactly one TRUE or FALSE
= means “assignment” and == means “comparison”
is.na() and !is.na() can be useful

title: Lecture 13
text:
Takeaways

You can read dplyr like a sentence: “Take the data, then filter, then group, then mutate, then summarize, then arrange…”
No $ signs or brackets: Inside dplyr verbs, you refer to columns by name directly (Foreign) rather than bom_base$Foreign.
Contextual Awareness: summarize() expects to perform the calculation within the groups created by the result of group_by(). In base R, aggregate() is a totally different function with its own unique syntax and usually requires the writing of custom functions.
dplyr will not drop dimensions (e.g., turning a single-column data frame into a vector), which is a common source of issues in base R.
The |> pipe was so popular in dplyr (originally as %>%) that the R core team actually added a “native” pipe (|>) to base R in version 4.1.0 because they realized how much it improved readability.
