title: Lecture 16
text:
Creation
Characters can be created using:

Single quotes (’’) or double quotes (““)

But double quotes are preferred in R

Have quotes within quotes?:

Single quotes go inside double quotes.


print("McDonald's")

[1] "McDonald's"


Double quotes within double quotes produce an error

print("This is an "error"")

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:20: unexpected symbol
1: print("This is an "error
                       ^


Double quotes inside double quotes require an escape character ("):

print("This is an \"error\" ")

[1] "This is an \"error\" "

title: Lecture 16
text:
Empty Characters as Container
To create a empty character vector to be filled:

character(10) # vector of 10 empty characters

 [1] "" "" "" "" "" "" "" "" "" ""



x <- character(10)
x <- strsplit("remarkable", split = "") |> unlist()
x

 [1] "r" "e" "m" "a" "r" "k" "a" "b" "l" "e"


But this is different from character(0) which creates an empty character vector for situations when you don’t know how many characters to expect.

my_vec <- character(0)
my_vec

character(0)


Example

for (word in c("banana", "banana", "meatball", "kiwi", "orange", "lemon")) {
  if (nchar(word) > 5) {
    my_vec <- c(my_vec, word)  # grow the vector as matches are found
  }
}

print(my_vec)

[1] "banana"   "banana"   "meatball" "orange"

title: Lecture 16
text:
print() v cat()

The print() function has an optional logical quote argument that specifies whether to print characters with or without quotation marks.


x <- "This is the \"R\" Language"
print(x) # same as just x in the console

[1] "This is the \"R\" Language"

print(x, quote = FALSE)

[1] This is the "R" Language

title: Lecture 16
text:
print() v cat()
The cat() function concatenates multiple character vectors into a single vector, adds a specified separator, and prints the result (without quotations).
cat(x, “check it out”, sep = “,”)

The printing is slightly different from that of quote(…, quote = FALSE).
The printed output does not have the vector index
The cat() function returns an invisible NULL (meaning assigning the printed output to a variable does not work).

title: Lecture 16
text:
The problem with strings

Strings are just messy
Differences due to capitalization and spelling differences (we vs. We are considered different words by R)
Differences because of punctuation and symbols (e.g., dedicate vs. dedicate, — are considered different words)
Differences because of conjugation, e.g., dedicated vs. dedicate vs. dedicates are considered 3 different words by R.
Any of these problems (or a combination of these problems) will make analysis with string characters that much more challenging.




tweet example

title: Lecture 16
text:
What is a regular expression?
Regular expression (AKA regex) is a symbolic notation system used to define search patterns within strings. Fuller discussion/lecture in Stats 102A

A formal language with defined syntax and rules.

Supported in most programming languages, including R.

Extremely flexible and powerful.

Common Applications:

Validate formats: Phone numbers, dates, emails, or passwords
Search and replace: Replace “Will”, “Bill”, or “W.” with “William”
Text processing: Identify spelling variations, count word combinations

title: Lecture 16
text:
Basics
Regular Expression Symbols:

. Matches any single character except a newline (wildcard)
ˆ Anchors the match to the start of a string. (starts with)

$ Anchors the match to the end of a string. (ends with)

\\ Escape special characters. (prevent error)

Can use Character Classes:
* [abc] Matches a, b, or c.
* [a-z] Matches any lowercase letter.
* [0-9] Matches any digit.
* [ˆabc] Matches any character except a, b, or c. (negate)
And Groups in strings:
* (abc) Matches the exact sequence “abc”.
* | Logical OR within a group.

* Matches 0 or more repetitions.
+ Matches 1 or more repetitions.
? Matches 0 or 1 repetition (makes it optional).
{n} Matches exactly n repetitions.
{n,} Matches n or more repetitions.
{n,m} Matches between n and m repetitions.

title: Lecture 16
text:
On Seeds/Pseudorandom numbers

Why “Pseudo” Random? It means “fake random”.
The numbers pass all the statistical tests for randomness — they’re spread out evenly, don’t repeat in obvious patterns, and behave like real random numbers — but they came from a formula, not true randomness.
If you don’t call set.seed(), R grabs something unpredictable from your computer — like the exact millisecond you ran the code — and uses that as the seed. That’s why your results look different each time you run a sample in R:


sample(1:100, 5)   

[1] 21 31 40 96 82

sample(1:100, 5)   

[1] 70  1 80 40 60

sample(1:100, 5)   

[1] 21 10 89  6 92

sample(1:100, 5)   

[1] 82 99 55 91 42

title: Lecture 16
text:
Why Should You Care?

Video games use pseudorandom numbers to generate maps, outcomes, behaviors
Cybersecurity uses them to generate encryption keys
AI and machine learning use them to shuffle training data and initialize models
Movies use them in visual effects to make simulated rain, fire, and crowds look natural

Randomness in computing is a clever illusion and we see it put to work in the discussion of distributions in Chapter 5 of Braun and Murdoch.

title: Lecture 16
text:
A little history

John Graunt (1661) took the step of tabulating data of deaths by age and ordering the ages from lowest to highest and produced the first “life table”.
While ordering data from low to high seems trivial today, it was not so trivial in the 1600s (imagine data on small scraps of paper).
And as other scientists begin tabling and graphing their data, this opened the way to examining probability distributions.
Graunt did not graph his data, but if he had, it would have revealed much about this population quickly.

title: Lecture 16
section: If Graunt had plotted his data
text: If Graunt had plotted his data

title: Lecture 16
text:
Some definitions for this section

Some definitions:

If a variable can assume any value between two specified values, it is called a continuous variable
Otherwise, it is called a discrete variable.

A probability distribution is a table or an equation that links each outcome of a statistical experiment with its probability or chance of occurrence. (Consider Graunt’s table - age at death & probability of death)
Probability distributions can be discrete or continuous too.

title: Lecture 16
text:
Some Properties

A discrete probability distribution can be tabled because its outcome can assume exact values (so Graunt made continuous age discrete by categorizing it).
A continuous variable cannot assume an exact value, that probability is zero. Therefore, continuous probability distributions are not tabled. Instead, formulas or ranges are used to describe probabilities.

A probability density function is an equation used to describe a continuous probability distribution.

title: Lecture 16
text:
R’s Probability Distributions

R’s probability distributions have four separate dedicated functions.
Each distribution has a root name. For example, the normal is “norm”. The binomial is “binom”
Also, the distribution functions in R operate in the same manner.
So if you learn one, you can figure out the others quickly.

title: Lecture 16
text: Commonly Seen

title: Lecture 16
text:
Distribution Generalities
All of the distributions in R have the following prefixes

r for “random”, a random variable having the specified distribution. This is the one you’ll use most often. It’s the simulator and will need to know how many you want.
d for “density”, the probability density function (p. d. f.), answers the question, “how likely is this value”
p for “probability”, the cumulative distribution function (c. d. f.), answers the question “what proportion falls below this value?”
q for “quantile”, the inverse c. d. f., the reverse of p given a proportion what value is associated with it.

title: Lecture 16

Example rnorm()

rnorm() has the syntax:
rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
Where n is a positive integer and is the length of the result.
rnorm() defaults to the standard normal (mean=0 and sd=1)
We can use it to generate random values from a normal distribution over a given range

title: Lecture 16
text:
Factors are variables in R which take on a limited number of different values, typically they are called non-numerical or “categorical” variables.
We use factors in statistical modeling because non-numerical variables (e.g., ancestry — African, Asian, European, Other) enter into statistical models differently than numerical variables.
Designating non-numerical data as factors insures that the modeling functions in R will treat these types of variables correctly.

title: Lecture 16
text:
Underneath a Factor

Factors in R are stored as a vector of integer values mapped to a corresponding set of character values. The character values are actually what gets displayed.
This is an efficient way to store character values, because each character value is stored only one time, and the data values are stored as a vector of integers. This requires far fewer computing resources.
This mechanism behind R’s factors and an AI’s chat window is the same: mapping human-readable text to machine-readable integers using a lookup dictionary.

title: Lecture 16
text:
Understanding

Computers cannot do math on letters. So whether you are estimating a model in R in 101A or interacting with Claude/ChatGPT/etc., the system requires numbers to do its job.
In R (Factors): If you have a column of survey data with “Low,” “Medium,” and “High,” R assigns integers to represent the values (e.g., 1, 2, 3). It then attaches a dictionary called levels to remember that 1 means “Low.” This mapping allows statistical algorithms (like regression) to perform calculations on categories.
In AI (Tokenization): When you type a sentence into a chat window, the AI chops your words into chunks and assigns each chunk an ID number (e.g., “The” = 464, “cat” = 3432). It aslo uses a dictionary to remember what each number meant. This mapping allows the underlying models to perform linear algebra on your prompt.
In both cases, integers are used as placeholder for a string to save memory and enable complex math.
Of course they diverge tremendously: AI chunks words into fragments (e.g., “un” “remark” “able”) and the numeric values assigned to the fragments have no order. The dictionaries AI uses are also massive (e.g., 100,000 times larger than a factor’s levels in R)

title: Lecture 16
text:
Additional Info regarding factors

We can create factors using factor() BUT ALSO R can automatically designate variables as factors during certain types of data import or other forms of data reading.
Both numeric and character variables can be converted into factors, but a factor’s values (known as levels) will always be displayed as character values - for example numbers will have quotes around them because they are being displayed as character
